newsitem.title: USA: Second US senator questions flow control's future.
newsitem.headline: Second US senator questions flow control's future.

text.p: A second key U.S. senator on Tuesday raised questions about whether Congress will pass legislation this year to protect billions of dollars of solid-waste facility debt.

"I said two years ago that I will tread cautiously with respect to interfering in the waste market," Sen. John Chafee, R-R-I., chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee said at a committee hearing on "flow control."
"This is still my view," Chafee said.
Flow control refers to the ability of local governments to direct solid waste to facilities within their borders that are financed with tax-exempt bonds.

The U.S. Supreme Court in 1994 said that flow control violates the U.S. Constitution because it impedes interstate trade. Fifteen tax-exempt bond issues have been downgraded since the High Court ruling.

Chafee said, "If we are going to take the dramatic step of granting federal permission for the creation of local trash monopolies that burden interstate commerce, I want to be sure that we are fixing an acute current problem."
"I also want to be sure that the cure is not worse than the problem we seek to solve," Chafee said.

Sen. Bob Smith, R-N.H., chairman of the Senate committee's subpanel on waste control, said in a written statement earlier on Tuesday that flow-control backers "have a much tougher case to prove this year."

Smith said, "During the last Congress, we had witnesses who testified that we had to act 'immediately' to protect municipalities from having to default on bonds they had issued to fund their waste-to-energy facilities, land fill construction and recycling efforts," Smith said.
"Now we are here two years later, and, surprise, surprise, the sky has not fallen," Smith said. "Municipal defaults did not occur."

Chafee said that 15 of the 18 credit rating downgrades that have occurred since the High Court ruling occurred in the first 12 months after the decision. "Relatively few have occurred in the two years since we last took testimony on this subject," he said.
